node.label: Jill Lepore
node.date_label: The Name of War (1998) · Historians Who Love Too Much (2001) · New York Burning (2005) · Book of Ages (2013) · These Truths (2018)
node.description: In The Name of War (1998), Jill Lepore argues that writing about King Philip’s War helped harden cultural boundaries and shape colonial American identity. She treats the words and later memories of war as historical forces, rather than simply records of violence. The book won the Bancroft Prize; Gordon S. Wood praised its imaginative scholarship but criticized its limited explanation of political, social and economic causes. In “Historians Who Love Too Much: Reflections on Microhistory and Biography” (2001), she reflects on the relation between the two genres. New York Burning (2005) extends her inquiry into slavery and political liberty, explicitly connected in her later account to Edmund Morgan’s American paradox. Book of Ages (2013) recovers Jane Franklin from little-studied documents, objects and portraits, while The Secret History of Wonder Woman (2014) places popular culture within feminist history. These Truths (2018) expands her work to a national synthesis. Her public writing has also provoked disagreement: Wood’s 2011 review of The Whites of Their Eyes (2010) faults her treatment of popular memory.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Name of War: King Philip’s War and the Origins of American Identity (1998); Historians Who Love Too Much: Reflections on Microhistory and Biography (2001); New York Burning: Liberty, Slavery, and Conspiracy in Eighteenth-Century Manhattan (2005); Blindspot, coauthored with Jane Kamensky (historical novel) (2008); The Whites of Their Eyes: The Tea Party’s Revolution and the Battle over American History (2010); Book of Ages: The Life and Opinions of Jane Franklin (2013); The Secret History of Wonder Woman (2014); These Truths: A History of the United States (2018).
node.scope_note: Selected primary passages of the 2001 methodological essay, the 2008 review and the 2009 interview were read. Selected passages of Wood’s 1998 review and the 2011 review were read. Monographs and the coauthored novel were not read in full; their arguments use identified publisher summaries, author testimony and named reception. Gelles’s Ulrich comparison was read only in the publisher’s review excerpt. The primary works by Davis, Morgan, Ulrich and Wood were not independently read. The 2026 revised These Truths and later books were not assessed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Wood criticizes The Name of War (1998) for giving too little explanatory weight to political, social and economic forces, and The Whites of Their Eyes (2010) for insufficient sympathy toward popular memory of the Revolution.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wood, The Bloodiest War (1998), paragraphs beginning “In this sort of postmodern history” and “Instead of composing”; No Thanks for the Memories (2011), paragraphs beginning “The Tea Partiers are certainly not scholars” and final paragraph. The first review also praises her imaginative scholarship. Both reviews read in these passages; neither book independently read in full. These are Wood’s judgments, not established defects.

proposed_edges.relationship: Discussing New York Burning (2005) in her 2009 interview, Lepore explicitly relates the entanglement of liberty and enslavement to Morgan’s American paradox.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: NEH interview, answer beginning “I’m interested in our capacity,” ending with the explicit attribution “American paradox” to Edmund Morgan. A named conceptual resource, not a supervision claim. Neither Morgan’s original formulation nor New York Burning was read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Book of Ages (2013), Edith B. Gelles places it in the historiographical line of Ulrich’s A Midwife’s Tale (1990) as a study of an obscure woman’s life.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Book of Ages publisher page, Praise, Gelles excerpt: “descends historiographically.” This is Gelles’s interpretation, not Lepore’s self-attribution. Full review and both books unread; Ulrich is another person in this run. The 1990 date of A Midwife’s Tale is also checked in Lepore 2001, p. 132, note 5.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reviewer links Book of Ages to A Midwife’s Tale

proposed_edges.relationship: Book of Ages: The Life and Opinions of Jane Franklin (2013) reconstructs the life of Benjamin Franklin’s obscure youngest sister from little-studied documents, objects and portraits.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher Book Description, paragraphs beginning “From one of our most accomplished” and “Making use”; Harvard biography, “absences and asymmetries.” This claim uses these summaries; the book was not read in full.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Name of War (1998) treats later remembrance of King Philip’s War as a force shaping American history, rather than merely a record of the conflict.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher Book Description, final two paragraphs; NEH interview, answers to the questions about American identity and later removal, especially “what’s remembered and what’s forgotten.” Argument read through publisher summary and author testimony; book body unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2009 interview, Lepore explains Common-place and the coauthored novel Blindspot (2008) as ways of bringing archival scholarship to public audiences and offering another interpretation of Boston’s historic sites.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: NEH interview, Common-place answers and answer to “Where and when?” about Park Service consulting: explicitly “public history.” Blindspot publisher metadata confirms 2008 and joint authorship with Jane Kamensky. This is her account of purpose, not evidence of audience reception; novel unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Archives, public audiences and historic sites

proposed_edges.relationship: The Secret History of Wonder Woman (2014) locates the superhero’s creation within the history of women’s rights, linking early suffrage campaigns with later feminism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher Book Description, paragraph beginning “The Secret History of Wonder Woman is a tour de force,” and original 2014 ebook date. The displayed 2015 paperback includes a later afterword. Publisher-mediated statement of argument; full book and afterword unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In These Truths: A History of the United States (2018), Jill Lepore attempted a national synthesis joining the country’s achievements and atrocities, which she explained in a 2019 interview as an alternative to opposed partisan histories.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s interview transcript. Lepore explains the intended synthesis and evidence-based civic purpose of her book. Claim concerns her stated intervention, not its success or other scholars’ adoption; the book itself was not read. The target is the national-narrative teaching umbrella, with no endorsement of imperial history implied.
